title: A credential that may read one field, and cannot go fishing
summary: Two credentials, same scope, same person. One is narrowed to a single attribute name - and that narrowing does not only refuse the other fields, it stops the credential looking anyone up by e-mail at all. Otherwise 200-versus-404 would still answer 'does this address exist here'.

steps.label: A person with several fields
steps.note: Registered by the full-access CRM credential.

steps.label: The full credential reads the e-mail
steps.note: Baseline: purpose stated, allowlist empty, so every field its purposes permit is readable.

steps.label: The narrowed credential reads its one allowed field
steps.note: This credential was created with an attribute allowlist of exactly loyalty_tier. Everything it is meant to do, it can do.

steps.label: The same credential cannot read the e-mail
steps.note: Same person, same scope, same purpose - refused, because the field is not on its list. The narrowing lives on the credential, not in the calling application.

steps.label: Nor the IBAN
steps.note: An allowlist is a list of what IS permitted, so a field nobody thought about is refused by default rather than exposed by default.

steps.label: And it cannot look anyone up by e-mail
steps.note: The subtle half. If lookup ignored the allowlist, this credential could still ask 'is ana@example.com in here' and read the answer off the 200-versus-404. So the allowlist gates lookup BY identifier kind too: no e-mail on the list, no lookup by e-mail.

steps.label: The full credential still can
steps.note: The refusal is a property of that credential, not of the endpoint - which is what makes narrowing a useful thing to hand to a job that only needs one number.

steps.label: A purpose it was never granted is refused
steps.note: Actions say WHAT, purposes say WHY, and the allowlist says WHICH FIELDS. All three are checked on every read - a credential is not a single switch.
